idea.before: Solving $a^0b^0-a^1b^1=0$ gives $b^0/b^1=a^1/a^0$, which is a reflection in the line $ct=x$. A boost rotates both arrows hyperbolically, i.e. it carries the mirror pair to another mirror pair, which is the invariance of $\eta(A,B)$ (rel-3.1). The Euclidean angle drawn on the page is therefore not meaningful: it is only $90^\circ$ when $A$ lies on a coordinate axis. The picture of a spacelike line orthogonal to a worldline is exactly the line of simultaneity of rel-1.6.
idea.after:
Solving $a^0b^0-a^1b^1=0$ gives $b^0/b^1=a^1/a^0$, which is a reflection in the line $ct=x$. A boost rotates both arrows hyperbolically, i.e. it carries the mirror pair to another mirror pair, which is the invariance of $\eta(A,B)$ (rel-3.1). The Euclidean angle drawn on the page is therefore not meaningful: it is only $90^\circ$ when $A$ lies on a coordinate axis. The picture of a spacelike line orthogonal to a worldline is exactly the line of simultaneity of rel-1.6.

For a nonzero $A\in\R^4$, the linear functional $T_A(B)=\eta(A,B)$ is nonzero because the metric is nondegenerate. Its range is therefore all of $\R$; rank-nullity (ladr 3.21) gives $\dim\ker T_A=4-1=3$. This is the orthogonal hyperplane. When $A$ is timelike, its rest frame makes the equation $B^0=0$, so every nonzero member is spacelike. For $A=0$, instead, the kernel is all of $\R^4$ and has dimension four. In the planar ratio above the denominators must be nonzero; the original linear equation, or $B=\lambda(a^1,a^0)$ for nonzero planar $A$, also handles the coordinate axes and $B=0$.

statement.before: The **four-acceleration** of a particle is $a^\mu=du^\mu/d\tau$. Differentiating $\eta(u,u)=c^2$ gives $\eta(a,u)=0$: $a$ is always Minkowski-orthogonal to $u$, hence spacelike (or zero). Its magnitude $\alpha=\sqrt{-\eta(a,a)}$ is the **proper acceleration**, the reading of an accelerometer carried by the particle. For motion along $x$ with lab acceleration $dv/dt$ one finds $\alpha=\gamma^3\,dv/dt$ (units $c=1$), and the four-acceleration is $a^\mu=\gamma^4\,(v\,\dot v,\ \dot v)$ in the components $(a^0,a^1)$.
statement.after: The **four-acceleration** of a particle is $a^\mu=du^\mu/d\tau$. Differentiating $\eta(u,u)=c^2$ gives $\eta(a,u)=0$: $a$ is always Minkowski-orthogonal to $u$, hence spacelike (or zero). Its magnitude $\alpha=\sqrt{-\eta(a,a)}$ is the **proper acceleration**, the reading of an accelerometer carried by the particle. For motion along $x$ with lab acceleration $dv/dt$ one finds $\alpha=\gamma^3\,|dv/dt|$ (units $c=1$), and the four-acceleration is $a^\mu=\gamma^4\,(v\,\dot v,\ \dot v)$ in the components $(a^0,a^1)$.

idea.before: Differentiate the identity $\eta(u,u)=c^2$ along the worldline: $2\eta(u,a)=0$. By rel-3.2, the vectors orthogonal to a timelike $u$ are spacelike, so $a$ is spacelike. In the instantaneous rest frame $u=(c,\mathbf 0)$ and $a^\mu=(0,\mathbf a_{\rm rest})$, where $\mathbf a_{\rm rest}$ is the ordinary acceleration there, which is what an on-board spring balance measures. In the lab, $a^1=\gamma\,d(\gamma v)/dt=\gamma^4\dot v$ and $a^0=\gamma\,d\gamma/dt=\gamma^4v\dot v$, so $\sqrt{(a^1)^2-(a^0)^2}=\gamma^4\dot v\sqrt{1-v^2}=\gamma^3\dot v$.
idea.after:
Differentiate the identity $\eta(u,u)=c^2$ along the worldline: $2\eta(u,a)=0$. By rel-3.2, every nonzero vector orthogonal to a timelike $u$ is spacelike, so $a$ is spacelike or zero. In the instantaneous rest frame $u=(c,\mathbf 0)$ and $a^\mu=(0,\mathbf a_{\rm rest})$, where $\mathbf a_{\rm rest}$ is the ordinary acceleration there, which is what an on-board spring balance measures. In the lab, $a^1=\gamma\,d(\gamma v)/dt=\gamma^4\dot v$ and $a^0=\gamma\,d\gamma/dt=\gamma^4v\dot v$, so $\sqrt{(a^1)^2-(a^0)^2}=\gamma^4|\dot v|\sqrt{1-v^2}=\gamma^3|\dot v|$.

In inertial coordinates the metric coefficients are constant. Apply the finite sum and product rules (pma 5.3) to the differentiable proper-time components in $(u^0)^2-\sum_{j=1}^3(u^j)^2=c^2$: their derivative is $2u^0a^0-2\sum_{j=1}^3u^ja^j=2\eta(u,a)=0$. This is a componentwise differentiation argument on any local proper-time interval of a smooth timelike worldline, distinct from converting lab-time derivatives by the chain rule (rel-3.4). A coordinate-dependent metric would contribute additional derivative terms; the displayed calculation uses a fixed inertial frame in flat spacetime.

caption.before: The same oscillating trip as in 3.4. Left: **slide the time**; the red arrow is $a$ (drawn at the scale shown in the readout when it is large), always the mirror image of $u$ in the light line, so $\eta(u,a)=0$. Right: the accelerometer reading $\alpha(t)$ (blue) against the lab acceleration $dv/dt$ (grey): at high speed the lab acceleration becomes tiny while the proper acceleration stays large by the factor $\gamma^3$.
caption.after: The same oscillating trip as in 3.4. Left: **slide the time**; the red arrow is $a$ (drawn at the scale shown in the readout when it is large), always the mirror image of $u$ in the light line, so $\eta(u,a)=0$. Right: the blue plot and its $\alpha$ readout use the **signed one-dimensional rest-frame acceleration** $\gamma^3\,dv/dt$, against the signed lab acceleration $dv/dt$ (grey). The nonnegative accelerometer magnitude defined above is the absolute value of that blue quantity; its sign records the chosen spatial direction. At zero lab acceleration both vanish; otherwise their magnitudes differ by the factor $\gamma^3$.
